question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To wish to go back to a previous point in the past in order to change or undo events or actions that are now regretted.
option_1: Turn back the hands of time
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Turn back the hands of time.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Turn back the hands of time" means to wish to go back to the past to change or undo events or actions now regretted.
◦ (पुराने समय में लौटने की इच्छा करना ताकि किसी पछतावे वाली घटना को बदला या मिटाया जा सके)

• This idiom is metaphorical and reflective and is commonly used when someone expresses regret over a past decision. (यह मुहावरा किसी बीते फैसले पर पछतावा व्यक्त करते समय प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Turn back the hands of time.

 

Additional Information

• Option 2: Against the clock (समय के विरुद्ध दौड़ते हुए): means working in a great hurry to meet a deadline.
◦ Example: The team was working against the clock to finish the report before midnight.

• Option 3: Time flies (समय पंख लगाकर उड़ता है): means that time passes very quickly.
◦ Example: Time flies when you are having fun with old friends.

• Option 4: In the nick of time (ऐन वक्त पर): means at the last possible moment, just in time.
◦ Example: The firefighters arrived in the nick of time to save the family.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A bad patch – Difficult period (कठिन समय)

2. A bolt from the blue – A sudden and unexpected event (एकदम अप्रत्याशित घटना)

3. A drop in the ocean – A very small amount compared to what is needed (आवश्यकता की तुलना में बहुत कम मात्रा)

4. A fish out of water – Someone who feels awkward in an unfamiliar situation (असहज स्थिति में व्यक्ति)

5. A piece of cake – Something very easy to do (बहुत आसान काम)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

Frustrated with the referee's biased decisions, the coach vowed ______ before the tournament ended.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To even the score.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "To even the score" means to avenge a wrong or make an unfair situation equal again, often in a competitive or personal context. (समान अन्याय का बदला लेना या स्थिति को बराबर करना)
◦ Example: After being cheated in the deal, she waited patiently for a chance to even the score.

 

• The completed sentence reads: Frustrated with the referee's biased decisions, the coach vowed to even the score before the tournament ended. This fits because the coach wants to make up for the unfair treatment his team suffered.

 

• The expression comes from the world of sports scoring, where a trailing team is said to "even the score" once it equals its opponent's tally.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "To even the ledger", "To even the tab" and "To even the count" — are not established English idioms at all. Each has been formed by simply replacing "score" with a similar-sounding word, and none of them carries any accepted meaning in English.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A storm in a teacup – Great fuss made over a trivial matter (छोटी बात पर बड़ा हंगामा)

2. Add fuel to the fire – To make a bad situation even worse (आग में घी डालना)

3. An axe to grind – A private or personal reason for doing something (निजी स्वार्थ रखना)

4. At the drop of a hat – Without any hesitation, immediately (बिना देर किए तुरंत)

5. Back to the drawing board – To start a plan over again from the beginning (योजना को नए सिरे से शुरू करना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

What goes around comes around.
option_1: Life moves in unpredictable cycles that no one can control.
option_2: What is lost will always be found again eventually.
option_3: One's actions—good or bad—will eventually have consequences that come back to that person.
option_4: Popular trends always return to fashion after some years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. One's actions—good or bad—will eventually have consequences that come back to that person..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "What goes around comes around" means that a person's actions, whether good or bad, will eventually return to affect them, reflecting a natural sense of moral consequence. (जैसी करनी वैसी भरनी)
◦ Example: He cheated his business partner for years, but what goes around comes around — he was cheated in return soon after.

 

• The phrase is often used as a warning or a reassurance about karma, emphasizing that one's own actions, rather than luck, determine what eventually happens to a person.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 wrongly generalizes the idiom into a statement about unpredictable life cycles, missing its specific link between one's own actions and their consequences.

 

• Option 2 confuses the idiom with expressions about lost objects reappearing, which is not what this idiom conveys.

 

• Option 4 misreads "comes around" literally as things recurring in fashion, rather than as consequences returning to the person who caused them.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Beat around the bush – To avoid speaking directly about something (सीधी बात न करना)

2. Bite the bullet – To face a difficult situation with courage (साहस के साथ कठिन स्थिति का सामना करना)

3. Break the ice – To initiate conversation in an awkward situation (असहज माहौल में बातचीत शुरू करना)

4. Burn the midnight oil – To work late into the night (देर रात तक काम करना)

5. By the skin of one's teeth – Very narrowly, just barely (बहुत मामूली अंतर से)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To be the first person to criticize or blame someone, especially when one is not without faults oneself.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Cast the first stone.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Cast the first stone" means to be the first person to criticize or blame someone, often despite having similar faults oneself.
◦ (सबसे पहले किसी की आलोचना या दोषारोपण करना, विशेषकर तब जब स्वयं भी दोषी हो)

• This idiom is biblical in origin and moralistic and is commonly used to caution people against judging others hypocritically. (यह मुहावरा दूसरों को पाखंडी तरीके से आंकने पर चेतावनी देने के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Cast the first stone.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Add fuel to the fire (आग में घी डालना): means to make an already bad situation worse.
◦ Example: Criticizing him publicly only added fuel to the fire during the dispute.

• Option 2: Rub salt in the wound (जख्मों पर नमक छिड़कना): means to make someone's suffering or embarrassment even worse.
◦ Example: Reminding her of the failure again was like rubbing salt in the wound.

• Option 3: Throw in the towel (हार मान लेना): means to give up or admit defeat.
◦ Example: After months of losses, the company decided to throw in the towel.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Call it a day – To stop working on something for the day (दिन का काम समाप्त करना)

2. Cut corners – To do something in the cheapest or easiest way, often sacrificing quality (गुणवत्ता से समझौता कर काम करना)

3. Cost an arm and a leg – To be extremely expensive (बहुत महंगा होना)

4. Cry over spilt milk – To worry uselessly about something that has already happened (हो चुकी बात पर व्यर्थ पछताना)

5. Curiosity killed the cat – Being too inquisitive can get one into trouble (जिज्ञासा मुसीबत में डाल सकती है)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

The tax forms were due at midnight, and he managed to submit his return just ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Under the wire.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Under the wire" means barely in time, at the very last moment, just before a deadline. (ऐन वक्त पर, आखिरी क्षण में)
◦ Example: She finished the assignment and emailed it under the wire, just minutes before the deadline.

 

• The completed sentence reads: The tax forms were due at midnight, and he managed to submit his return just under the wire. The phrase fits because it stresses how narrowly he met the deadline.

 

• The expression comes from horse racing, where a wire once stretched across the finish line, and a horse winning "under the wire" had barely crossed in time.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "On the fence" (undecided or neutral about an issue), "Down the line" (at some point in the future) and "In hot water" (in trouble or facing difficulty) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of narrowly meeting a deadline required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Cut to the chase – To get to the point without wasting time (बिना समय गंवाए मुद्दे पर आना)

2. Devil's advocate – Someone who argues the opposing side just for the sake of debate (जान-बूझकर विपरीत पक्ष रखने वाला)

3. Down to the wire – Continuing until the very last possible moment (अंतिम क्षण तक चलना)

4. Eat humble pie – To admit one's mistake and apologize (गलती स्वीकार कर माफी माँगना)

5. Every cloud has a silver lining – There is something good in every bad situation (हर बुरी स्थिति में कुछ अच्छा भी होता है)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

A fate worse than death.
option_1: A situation involving actual physical danger to one's life.
option_2: A situation or experience that is extremely unpleasant or distressing, though not literally fatal.
option_3: An outcome that directly leads to someone's death.
option_4: A punishment reserved only for serious criminals.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A situation or experience that is extremely unpleasant or distressing, though not literally fatal..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "A fate worse than death" means a situation or experience that is extremely unpleasant, humiliating, or distressing, even though it does not literally involve dying. (मृत्यु से भी बदतर स्थिति)
◦ Example: Losing her reputation in the small town felt like a fate worse than death to her.

 

• The phrase is often used hyperbolically for dramatic effect, so the "worse than death" part should not be read literally as involving actual danger to life.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 wrongly interprets the idiom literally as physical danger to life, when the phrase is actually used hyperbolically for extreme unpleasantness.

 

• Option 3 confuses the idiom with an outcome that causes death, whereas the idiom specifically describes something that feels worse than dying without anyone actually dying.

 

• Option 4 narrows the idiom incorrectly to criminal punishment, though it is used broadly for any deeply distressing personal situation.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Get a taste of your own medicine – To be treated the way one treats others (जैसा किया वैसा भरना)

2. Give someone the cold shoulder – To ignore someone deliberately (जान-बूझकर अनदेखा करना)

3. Go the extra mile – To make a special extra effort (अतिरिक्त प्रयास करना)

4. Hit the nail on the head – To describe exactly what is causing a situation (बिल्कुल सही बात कहना)

5. Hit the sack – To go to bed (सोने जाना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To express one's opinion or disapproval of something by choosing to leave, stay away, or stop participating, rather than by speaking out.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Vote with one's feet.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Vote with one's feet" means to express one's opinion or disapproval of something by leaving, staying away, or ceasing to participate, rather than by voicing it directly.
◦ (अपनी राय को शब्दों में नहीं बल्कि वहाँ से चले जाने या दूर रहने के जरिए ज़ाहिर करना)

• This idiom is figurative and originally political and is commonly used to describe consumers or citizens showing disapproval through their actions rather than speech. (यह मुहावरा उपभोक्ताओं या नागरिकों द्वारा शब्दों के बजाय कार्यों से असहमति दिखाने के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Vote with one's feet.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Sit on the fence (तटस्थ रहना, पक्ष न लेना): means to avoid taking sides on an issue.
◦ Example: He refused to sit on the fence and openly supported the new policy.

• Option 2: Toe the line (नियमों का पालन करना): means to conform to a rule or standard expected by a group.
◦ Example: New employees are expected to toe the line set by company policy.

• Option 4: Jump on the bandwagon (लोकप्रिय प्रवृत्ति में शामिल होना): means to join others in doing something currently fashionable or popular.
◦ Example: Many companies jumped on the bandwagon of eco-friendly packaging.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. It's raining cats and dogs – Raining very heavily (मूसलाधार बारिश होना)

2. Keep an eye on – To watch someone or something carefully (ध्यान से नज़र रखना)

3. Kill two birds with one stone – To achieve two things with a single action (एक तीर से दो शिकार करना)

4. Let the cat out of the bag – To reveal a secret accidentally (राज़ खोल देना)

5. Once in a blue moon – Very rarely (कभी-कभार)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

The manager barked at the new intern to finish the report ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Tout de suite.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Tout de suite" means immediately, right away, without any delay, borrowed directly from French into everyday English usage. (तुरंत, फ़ौरन)
◦ Example: The captain ordered the sailors to lower the sails tout de suite as the storm approached.

 

• The completed sentence reads: The manager barked at the new intern to finish the report tout de suite. This fits because the manager is demanding instant action, not a delayed response.

 

• The expression comes from French, where "tout de suite" literally means "in succession" but is used colloquially to mean "right now."

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "In the long run" (over an extended period of time), "At a snail's pace" (very slowly) and "On second thought" (after reconsidering a decision) — are all genuine idiomatic expressions, but none of them fits the sense of immediate urgency required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. On thin ice – In a risky or precarious situation (जोखिम भरी स्थिति में)

2. Pull someone's leg – To joke or tease someone playfully (मज़ाक करना)

3. Put all your eggs in one basket – To risk everything on a single plan (सब कुछ एक ही योजना पर दांव पर लगाना)

4. Rain check – To postpone an invitation or plan to a later time (योजना को टालना)

5. Read between the lines – To understand a hidden or implied meaning (छिपे अर्थ को समझना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Tide someone over.
option_1: To help someone get through a difficult period, typically by providing money or resources until things improve.
option_2: To rescue someone from drowning in a river or the sea.
option_3: To postpone a decision until a more favourable time.
option_4: To gradually persuade someone to change their opinion.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To help someone get through a difficult period, typically by providing money or resources until things improve..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Tide someone over" means to help someone manage through a difficult period, usually by lending money or resources until conditions improve. (किसी की कठिन समय में मदद करना, प्रायः पैसे उधार देकर)
◦ Example: His uncle lent him some cash to tide him over until his next salary arrived.

 

• The phrase draws on the image of a "tide" carrying someone safely through rough water, so the emphasis is on temporary support rather than a permanent solution.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 takes the word "tide" too literally, treating the idiom as if it referred to an actual rescue from water rather than financial or practical support.

 

• Option 3 confuses the idiom with expressions about delaying decisions, whereas "tide someone over" is about sustaining a person, not postponing a choice.

 

• Option 4 wrongly links the idiom to persuasion or changing opinions, which has no connection to its actual meaning of temporary support.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Ring a bell – To sound familiar (परिचित लगना)

2. See eye to eye – To agree completely with someone (सहमत होना)

3. Sit on the fence – To avoid taking sides on an issue (पक्ष न लेना)

4. Speak of the devil – Said when the very person just mentioned suddenly appears (जिसकी बात हो रही हो वह अचानक आ जाए)

5. Spill the beans – To reveal secret information (राज़ उजागर करना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To enjoy oneself immensely, having a thoroughly good and fun time.
option_2: Have a whale of a time
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Have a whale of a time.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Have a whale of a time" means to enjoy oneself immensely, having a thoroughly good and fun experience.
◦ (बहुत आनंद उठाना, खूब मज़ा करना)

• This idiom is informal and exaggerative, using "whale" to suggest something large or huge, and is commonly used to describe memorable outings or parties. (यह मुहावरा यादगार सैर या पार्टियों का वर्णन करने के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Have a whale of a time.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Kill time (समय बिताना): means to pass time doing something unimportant while waiting for something else.
◦ Example: We played cards to kill time at the airport.

• Option 3: Call it a day (दिन का काम समाप्त करना): means to stop working on something for the day.
◦ Example: After eight hours at the office, the team decided to call it a day.

• Option 4: Burn the midnight oil (देर रात तक काम करना): means to work late into the night, usually to finish something important.
◦ Example: She had to burn the midnight oil to complete the project before the deadline.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Take with a grain of salt – To not take something too seriously or literally (पूरी तरह विश्वास न करना)

2. The ball is in your court – It is now your turn to act or decide (अब निर्णय तुम्हारा है)

3. Throw in the towel – To give up on something (हार मान लेना)

4. Under the weather – Feeling slightly unwell (अस्वस्थ महसूस करना)

5. Up in the air – Still undecided or uncertain (अनिश्चित)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

The comedian's tasteless joke about the tragedy was enough to ______ everyone in the audience.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Make one's toes curl.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Make one's toes curl" means to cause someone an acute feeling of disgust, shame, or embarrassment, often through something cringe-worthy. (किसी को शर्मिंदगी या घिन का गहरा एहसास कराना)
◦ Example: His awkward attempt at flattery made her toes curl with embarrassment.

 

• The completed sentence reads: The comedian's tasteless joke about the tragedy was enough to make everyone's toes curl in the audience. This fits because the joke provoked a strong reaction of embarrassment and discomfort.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "Make one's fingers curl", "Make one's ears curl" and "Make one's knees curl" — are not established English idioms at all. Each has been formed by simply replacing "toes" with another body part, and none of them carries any accepted meaning in English.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A blessing in disguise – Something that seems bad at first but turns out well (जो बुरा लगे पर अच्छा साबित हो)

2. Bark up the wrong tree – To pursue a mistaken course of action (गलत दिशा में प्रयास करना)

3. Break a leg – A way of wishing someone good luck (शुभकामनाएँ देना)

4. Elephant in the room – An obvious problem that no one wants to mention (स्पष्ट समस्या जिसका कोई ज़िक्र नहीं करता)

5. Face the music – To accept the consequences of one's actions (परिणाम भुगतना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Turn the tide.
option_1: To flow with ocean currents in a predictable pattern.
option_2: To postpone an event until conditions become favourable.
option_3: To follow the majority opinion in a group.
option_4: To dramatically change or reverse the direction or outcome of a situation, especially in a contest or struggle.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To dramatically change or reverse the direction or outcome of a situation, especially in a contest or struggle..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "Turn the tide" means to dramatically change or reverse the direction of events, especially in a battle, contest, or struggle that seemed to be going against someone. (स्थिति को नाटकीय रूप से पलट देना)
◦ Example: A brilliant second-half strategy helped the underdog team turn the tide and win the match.

 

• The idiom draws on the literal image of an ocean tide turning direction, and is most often used in contexts of sports, politics, or conflict where momentum shifts suddenly.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 takes the word "tide" too literally, describing ocean currents rather than a dramatic reversal in a situation.

 

• Option 2 confuses the idiom with postponing an event, whereas "turn the tide" is about reversing momentum, not delaying it.

 

• Option 3 wrongly links the idiom to following the majority, which is closer to a different expression such as "go with the flow" and not the meaning of this idiom.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Get out of hand – To become uncontrollable (काबू से बाहर होना)

2. Go back to square one – To start over from the very beginning (शुरुआत से आरंभ करना)

3. Hang in there – To remain persistent despite difficulty (डटे रहना)

4. Hit the books – To study hard (मन लगाकर पढ़ना)

5. In the same boat – Facing the same difficult situation as someone else (समान कठिन स्थिति में होना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To satisfy or fulfill everything that is necessary or desired for a particular purpose.
option_3: Go back to the drawing board
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Tick all the boxes.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Tick all the boxes" means to satisfy or fulfill everything that is necessary or desired.
◦ (हर ज़रूरी शर्त को पूरी तरह पूरा करना)

• This idiom is a modern, checklist-style expression and is commonly used to describe a candidate, plan or product that meets every requirement perfectly. (यह किसी उम्मीदवार, योजना या उत्पाद के सभी मानकों पर खरा उतरने के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Tick all the boxes.

 

Additional Information

• Option 2: Cut corners (काम को सस्ते या घटिया तरीके से करना): to do something in the easiest or cheapest way, often lowering its quality.
◦ Example: The builder cut corners on safety, and the wall collapsed.

• Option 3: Go back to the drawing board (नए सिरे से योजना बनाना): to start planning something again from scratch after an earlier attempt has failed.
◦ Example: When the prototype failed the test, the team went back to the drawing board.

• Option 4: Raise the bar (मानक को ऊँचा उठाना): to set a higher standard of performance than existed before.
◦ Example: The champion's record-breaking run raised the bar for future athletes.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A bad patch – Difficult period (कठिन समय)

2. A bed of roses – An easy, comfortable situation (सुखद और आरामदायक स्थिति)

3. A blessing in disguise – Something that seems bad but turns out to be good (आपदा में अवसर)

4. A close shave – A narrow escape from danger (बाल-बाल बचना)

5. A cock and bull story – An unbelievable, made-up story (गप्प कहानी)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

Despite losing her job and her home in the same month, she remained a ______ and rebuilt her life within a year.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Tough cookie.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "tough cookie" means a person who is strong, resilient, and not easily defeated, even in difficult circumstances. (एक मज़बूत और दृढ़ स्वभाव का व्यक्ति जो आसानी से हार नहीं मानता)
◦ Example: Losing the first round didn't faze her; she's always been a tough cookie.

 

• The completed sentence reads: Despite losing her job and her home in the same month, she remained a tough cookie and rebuilt her life within a year. Only this phrase conveys the resilience needed to bounce back from repeated setbacks.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "Soft touch" (someone who is easily persuaded or taken advantage of), "Wet blanket" (someone who spoils other people's fun or enthusiasm) and "Fair-weather friend" (someone who is loyal only when things are going well) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of quiet strength and resilience required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A drop in the ocean – A very small amount compared to what is needed (ऊंट के मुंह में जीरा)

2. A fish out of water – Feeling awkward in unfamiliar surroundings (असहज स्थिति में होना)

3. A pain in the neck – An annoying person or thing (परेशान करने वाला व्यक्ति या चीज़)

4. A piece of cake – Something very easy to do (बहुत आसान काम)

5. A red-letter day – A memorable and happy day (यादगार दिन)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

To have a finger in every pie.
option_1: To be extremely skilled at cooking a variety of dishes.
option_2: To interfere in matters that do not concern oneself.
option_3: To be involved in numerous different activities, projects, or businesses at the same time.
option_4: To keep a small share of every profit made by others.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. To be involved in numerous different activities, projects, or businesses at the same time..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "to have a finger in every pie" means to be involved in numerous different activities, projects, or businesses at the same time, often to control or influence outcomes. (हर काम में हाथ डालना, कई गतिविधियों में शामिल होना)
◦ Example: As the town's mayor, local businessman, and newspaper owner, he has a finger in every pie.

 

• The word pie here symbolises any venture or enterprise, not literally food, so the phrase is entirely figurative and should not be confused with idioms about cooking or sharing profits.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 confuses the figurative "pie" with an actual dessert, wrongly reading the idiom as being about cooking skill rather than involvement in ventures.

 

• Option 2 narrows the meaning to unwanted meddling alone, whereas the idiom simply describes broad involvement, which may be entirely welcome or professional.

 

• Option 4 mixes this idiom up with the unrelated expression "a piece of the pie", which is about receiving a share of profit, not about being active in many activities.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A shot in the arm – Something that provides encouragement or a boost (प्रोत्साहन देने वाली चीज़)

2. A slap on the wrist – A very mild punishment (हल्की सी सजा)

3. A storm in a teacup – Great fuss made over a trivial matter (राई का पहाड़ बनाना)

4. A wild goose chase – A futile and hopeless search (व्यर्थ की खोज)

5. Add fuel to the fire – To make a bad situation worse (आग में घी डालना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

Feeling slightly unwell, sick, or in low spirits.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Under the weather.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Under the weather" means slightly unwell or in low spirits.
◦ (थोड़ा अस्वस्थ या उदास महसूस करना)

• This idiom is a classic exam idiom and is commonly used when someone has a mild illness like a cold, rather than a serious disease. (यह मुहावरा हल्की बीमारी, जैसे ज़ुकाम, के लिए प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Under the weather.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Over the moon (बहुत खुश होना): to be extremely happy or delighted about something.
◦ Example: She was over the moon when she heard she had topped the exam.

• Option 2: In high spirits (उत्साहित और प्रसन्न): to be cheerful, energetic, and in a good mood.
◦ Example: The whole team was in high spirits after their victory.

• Option 3: Full of beans (ऊर्जा से भरपूर): to be lively, energetic, and enthusiastic.
◦ Example: The children were full of beans on the first day of the holidays.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Back to the wall – In a desperate, defensive situation (मुश्किल स्थिति में फंसा होना)

2. Bark up the wrong tree – To pursue a mistaken course of action (गलत दिशा में प्रयास करना)

3. Beat around the bush – To avoid talking directly about the main issue (इधर-उधर की बातें करना)

4. Behind the scenes – Privately, away from public view (पर्दे के पीछे)

5. Bite the bullet – To face a difficult or unpleasant situation with courage (कठिन परिस्थिति का साहसपूर्वक सामना करना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

After weeks of unannounced visits and endless demands on his cousin's hospitality, it became clear that Ravi was beginning to ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Wear out one's welcome.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "wear out one's welcome" means to stay as a guest for so long, or to visit so often, that the host no longer wants you there, even though nothing may be said openly. (किसी के घर बहुत देर तक या बार-बार रुककर मेज़बान का धैर्य समाप्त कर देना)
◦ Example: The relatives stayed for three weeks and clearly wore out their welcome.

 

• The completed sentence reads: After weeks of unannounced visits and endless demands on his cousin's hospitality, it became clear that Ravi was beginning to wear out his welcome. The repeated, excessive visits are exactly what the idiom describes.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "Give someone the cold shoulder" (to deliberately ignore or be unfriendly towards someone), "Show someone the ropes" (to teach someone how a task or job is done) and "Bring home the bacon" (to earn the money needed to support one's family) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of overstaying one's hospitality required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Bite the dust – To fail, be defeated, or die (असफल होना या मारा जाना)

2. Break the ice – To initiate conversation in an awkward situation (बातचीत की शुरुआत करना)

3. Burn the midnight oil – To work late into the night (देर रात तक मेहनत से काम करना)

4. By hook or by crook – By any means, fair or unfair (किसी भी तरह से, उचित या अनुचित)

5. Call it a day – To decide to stop working on something (काम को यहीं समाप्त करना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Tied to one's apron strings.
option_1: Forced to do household chores against one's will.
option_2: Excessively dependent on or controlled by another person, especially one's mother.
option_3: Romantically attached to a much older partner.
option_4: Financially supported entirely by a spouse's income.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Excessively dependent on or controlled by another person, especially one's mother..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "tied to one's apron strings" means excessively dependent on or controlled by another person, especially one's mother, and unable to act independently. (किसी पर, विशेषकर माँ पर, अत्यधिक निर्भर या नियंत्रित होना)
◦ Example: At thirty, he was still tied to his mother's apron strings and could not make a single decision alone.

 

• The image comes from a young child literally clinging to the strings of a mother's apron, so the idiom is almost always used about excessive dependence, most commonly on a mother, rather than about any other kind of relationship.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 takes the word "apron" literally, wrongly turning the idiom into a statement about doing housework rather than about emotional or practical dependence.

 

• Option 3 confuses dependence with romance, but the idiom carries no suggestion of a romantic relationship at all.

 

• Option 4 narrows the dependence to money alone, whereas the idiom covers overall control and lack of independence, not just financial support.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Cast iron stomach – Able to eat or endure anything without being affected (कुछ भी पचा लेने की क्षमता)

2. Cost an arm and a leg – To be extremely expensive (बहुत महंगा होना)

3. Cry over spilt milk – To worry uselessly about something that has already happened (बीती बात पर पछताना)

4. Cut the mustard – To meet the required standard (अपेक्षित मानक पर खरा उतरना)

5. Down to earth – Practical, sensible and unpretentious (सरल और व्यावहारिक स्वभाव का)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

To pay someone money, especially as a bribe or reward for doing something.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Cross one's palm with silver.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Cross one's palm with silver" means to pay someone, especially as a bribe or a reward for a favour.
◦ (किसी को घूस या इनाम के तौर पर पैसे देना)

• This idiom is an old-fashioned, slightly literary expression and is commonly used when talking about paying a fortune-teller, an official, or anyone whose cooperation is being bought. (यह मुहावरा भविष्यवक्ता, अधिकारी आदि को घूस देने के संदर्भ में प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Cross one's palm with silver.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: Foot the bill (बिल या खर्च का भुगतान करना): to pay the cost of something, such as a meal or an event.
◦ Example: The company agreed to foot the bill for the entire conference.

• Option 2: Cost a pretty penny (बहुत महंगा पड़ना): to be very expensive.
◦ Example: That antique clock must have cost a pretty penny.

• Option 4: Break the bank (सारा पैसा खर्च हो जाना, बहुत महंगा पड़ना): to use up all of one's available money, or to be prohibitively expensive.
◦ Example: A weekend trip to that resort would break the bank for most students.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Draw a blank – To fail to remember or find something (कुछ भी याद न आना)

2. Eat humble pie – To admit one's mistake and apologize humbly (अपनी गलती स्वीकार कर माफी माँगना)

3. Face the music – To accept criticism or punishment for one's actions (आलोचना या दंड का सामना करना)

4. Get cold feet – To lose one's courage or nerve just before doing something (अंतिम समय में हिम्मत हार जाना)

5. Give someone the benefit of the doubt – To trust someone's word without full proof (बिना पूरे प्रमाण के भरोसा करना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

The wealthy alumnus donated a large sum to the school library, insisting that the gift came ______.
option_1: At the drop of a hat
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. With no strings attached.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "with no strings attached" means given freely, without any hidden conditions, obligations, or restrictions, so the receiver owes nothing in return. (बिना किसी शर्त या बंधन के दिया गया)
◦ Example: The grant came with no strings attached, so the researchers could spend it however they judged best.

 

• The completed sentence reads: The wealthy alumnus donated a large sum to the school library, insisting that the gift came with no strings attached. This matches the idea of a donation given without demanding anything in return.

 

• The expression comes from the image of a puppet controlled by strings — a gift "with no strings" cannot be secretly controlled or called back by the giver.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "At the drop of a hat" (immediately, without any hesitation or delay), "Once in a blue moon" (very rarely) and "Through thick and thin" (through all circumstances, good or bad, out of loyalty) — are all genuine idioms, but none of them fits the sense of an unconditional gift required by this sentence.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Go the extra mile – To make an additional effort beyond what is expected (अपेक्षा से अधिक प्रयास करना)

2. Hit the nail on the head – To describe exactly what is causing a situation or problem (ठीक निशाने पर बात कहना)

3. Hit the sack – To go to bed (सोने चले जाना)

4. In the same boat – Facing the same difficult situation as someone else (एक ही जैसी परिस्थिति में होना)

5. Jump on the bandwagon – To join others in doing something that has become popular (लोकप्रिय प्रवृत्ति में शामिल हो जाना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

The penny drops.
option_1: Someone suddenly understands or realizes something that had previously been unclear.
option_2: A small amount of money is unexpectedly found or received.
option_3: A long-awaited piece of good news finally arrives.
option_4: A plan or scheme ultimately fails and has to be abandoned.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Someone suddenly understands or realizes something that had previously been unclear..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "the penny drops" means someone suddenly understands or realizes something after a period of confusion, as if a coin has finally fallen into place inside a machine. (अचानक किसी बात को समझ या भाँप जाना)
◦ Example: I explained the joke twice before the penny finally dropped and she started laughing.

 

• The phrase comes from old coin-operated slot machines, which worked only once the inserted penny fell into place, so it is used purely about sudden understanding, never about money itself, despite the literal wording.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 takes the word "penny" literally as money, ignoring that the idiom is entirely about a moment of mental realization.

 

• Option 3 confuses sudden understanding with the arrival of awaited news, but the idiom is about insight, not about receiving information from outside.

 

• Option 4 wrongly links the phrase to failure or abandonment of a plan, which is not part of the idiom's meaning at all.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. Keep an eye on – To watch someone or something carefully (किसी पर नज़र रखना)

2. Kick the bucket – To die (मर जाना)

3. Kill two birds with one stone – To achieve two things with a single action (एक तीर से दो शिकार करना)

4. Let the cat out of the bag – To reveal a secret, often by accident (राज़ खोल देना)

5. Turn over a new leaf – To start behaving in a better, more responsible way (नए सिरे से अच्छा आचरण अपनाना)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

A minor flaw, drawback, or detrimental detail that spoils an otherwise good situation or plan.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A fly in the ointment.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "A fly in the ointment" means a small flaw or drawback that spoils an otherwise good or promising situation.
◦ (किसी अच्छी स्थिति में एक छोटी सी खामी जो सब कुछ बिगाड़ दे)

• This idiom is a classic, slightly old-fashioned exam idiom and is commonly used when one small negative detail threatens to ruin an otherwise successful plan. (यह मुहावरा तब प्रयोग होता है जब एक छोटी सी बात पूरी अच्छी योजना को बिगाड़ दे)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A fly in the ointment.

 

Additional Information

• Option 1: A drop in the ocean (ऊंट के मुंह में जीरा, यानी बहुत कम मात्रा): an amount so small compared to what is needed that it makes almost no difference.
◦ Example: The donation was generous, but compared to the total cost of rebuilding the school, it was a drop in the ocean.

• Option 3: A blessing in disguise (मुसीबत में भी छिपा कोई लाभ): something that initially seems unfortunate but eventually turns out to be beneficial.
◦ Example: Losing that job was a blessing in disguise, as it led her to start her own successful business.

• Option 4: A storm in a teacup (राई का पहाड़ बनाना, यानी छोटी बात का बतंगड़): a great deal of fuss or anger made about something trivial or unimportant.
◦ Example: The whole office argument turned out to be a storm in a teacup.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. On thin ice – In a risky or precarious situation (जोखिम भरी स्थिति में)

2. Out of the blue – Suddenly and unexpectedly (अचानक, बिना किसी संकेत के)

3. Pull someone's leg – To tease or joke with someone (किसी का मज़ाक उड़ाना)

4. Read between the lines – To understand a hidden or implied meaning (छिपे हुए अर्थ को समझना)

5. Rings a bell – Sounds familiar, reminds one of something (जाना-पहचाना सा लगना)

question:
Fill in the blank with the correct idiom selecting from the given alternatives.

Everyone said the old shopkeeper was impossible to fool, so getting the better of him even once felt like managing to ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Catch a weasel asleep.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "catch a weasel asleep" means to surprise or catch off guard someone who is normally very alert, cunning, or watchful, since a weasel is proverbially difficult to catch napping. (किसी बहुत सतर्क व्यक्ति को असावधान पकड़ लेना)
◦ Example: Fooling the old customs officer was so hard that colleagues joked you'd sooner catch a weasel asleep.

 

• The completed sentence reads: Everyone said the old shopkeeper was impossible to fool, so getting the better of him even once felt like managing to catch a weasel asleep. The comparison fits because both describe outsmarting someone famously alert.

 

• The expression comes from the real habits of the weasel, an animal long regarded in folklore as being permanently watchful and almost never caught off guard.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The remaining alternatives — "Catch a rabbit asleep", "Catch a squirrel asleep" and "Catch a hedgehog asleep" — are not established English idioms at all. Each has been formed by simply replacing "weasel" with another small animal, and none of them carries any accepted meaning in English.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. See eye to eye – To agree completely with someone (पूरी तरह सहमत होना)

2. Sit on the fence – To remain neutral and avoid taking sides (तटस्थ रहना, पक्ष न लेना)

3. Spill the beans – To reveal secret information, often accidentally (राज़ खोल देना)

4. Steal someone's thunder – To take credit for someone else's achievement (किसी की उपलब्धि का श्रेय खुद ले लेना)

5. Take with a pinch of salt – To not fully believe something one is told (किसी बात पर पूरा विश्वास न करना)

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

Albatross around one's neck.
option_1: A lucky charm that brings good fortune to its owner.
option_2: A minor inconvenience that is quickly forgotten.
option_3: A well-deserved reward for past achievements.
option_4: A persistent burden or source of guilt that is very difficult to get rid of.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A persistent burden or source of guilt that is very difficult to get rid of..

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "albatross around one's neck" means a heavy, persistent burden, obligation, or source of guilt that is very hard to escape. (गले की हड्डी बन जाना, यानी न छूटने वाला भारी बोझ)
◦ Example: The failed business loan became an albatross around his neck for the next ten years.

 

• The phrase comes from Samuel Taylor Coleridge's poem The Rime of the Ancient Mariner, in which a sailor who kills an albatross is forced to wear its corpse around his neck as a punishment, so the idiom carries a strong sense of guilt as well as burden.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 reverses the idiom's meaning, treating the albatross as a symbol of good luck rather than as the heavy, guilt-laden burden the phrase actually describes.

 

• Option 2 understates the idiom by calling it a minor, quickly forgotten problem, whereas the whole point of the phrase is that the burden is serious and hard to shake off.

 

• Option 3 wrongly turns a burden into something positive and earned, when the idiom describes an unwanted weight, not a reward.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. The ball is in your court – It is now your turn to take action or make a decision (अब निर्णय लेने की बारी तुम्हारी है)

2. Throw in the towel – To give up or admit defeat (हार मान लेना)

3. Turn a blind eye – To deliberately ignore something one should notice (जानबूझकर अनदेखा करना)

4. Under a cloud – Under suspicion or in disgrace (शक या बदनामी के घेरे में)

5. Up in the air – Undecided or uncertain (अनिश्चित, हवा में लटका हुआ)

question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

An exorbitant or extremely large sum of money.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. King's ransom.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "King's ransom" means an exorbitant sum of money.
◦ (बहुत बड़ी रकम)

• This idiom is a classic exam idiom and is commonly used to describe something that costs or is worth a huge amount. (किसी चीज़ के बहुत महंगा या बेशकीमती होने के संदर्भ में प्रयोग होता है)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. King's ransom.

 

Additional Information

• Option 2: A drop in the bucket (ऊंट के मुंह में जीरा): an amount so small that it makes little difference to a larger problem.
◦ Example: The donation was generous, but compared to the total cost of rebuilding the school, it was just a drop in the bucket.

• Option 3: Money for old rope (बिना मेहनत की कमाई): payment received for very little effort or something of little value.
◦ Example: Getting paid to proofread one page was money for old rope.

• Option 4: Break the bank (बहुत ज़्यादा खर्च कर देना): to cost so much that it uses up all one's available money.
◦ Example: Buying a new laptop won't exactly break the bank, so I can afford it.

 

5 Important Idioms

1. A bad patch – A difficult or unlucky period (कठिन समय)

2. A blessing in disguise – Something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good (छिपा हुआ वरदान)

3. A drop in the ocean – A very small amount compared to what is needed (ऊंट के मुंह में जीरा)

4. A piece of cake – Something very easy to do (बहुत आसान काम)

5. A storm in a teacup – A great deal of fuss over something trivial (बात का बतंगड़)
